title: GridWatch
subtitle: Power outage prediction & grid equipment failure advisor
body:
U1 / IBM Bobathon 2026
A working local prototype for grid decision support
notes: GridWatch helps an operator examine equipment risk, compare weather scenarios and prepare maintenance work. The presentation distinguishes the real temperature forecast from the separate synthetic outage classifier. The project is a local prototype, not a field-validated outage prediction service. Industrial images are AI-generated illustrations of fictional facilities. Source: supplied Industry Problem Statements - 2026.pdf, U1; docs/model-card.md.

title: The maintenance decision
subtitle: Equipment condition is only part of the problem
body:
A sensor warning does not explain which asset should be serviced first. Operators also need weather exposure, customer impact and available resources.

U1 asks for an advisor that identifies outage-prone equipment and areas, ranks their consequences and prepares a maintenance and crew-positioning plan.
notes: Calendar-based maintenance does not directly use current equipment condition. The U1 brief proposes combining temperature, vibration, partial discharge and oil quality with weather and incident history. GridWatch demonstrates that decision workflow. We have not measured actual avoided outages, monetary savings or utility response-time improvements. Source: supplied Industry Problem Statements - 2026.pdf, U1. Photo: src/web/grid-engineers.png, AI-generated illustration.

title: How GridWatch works
subtitle: A shared analysis engine connects models to decisions
body:
An operator enters wind, rainfall and crew availability. The saved classifier estimates each fictional asset’s next-day failure risk.

The advisor combines risk with service impact, creates a priority queue and proposes jobs that fit crew skills and shift capacity.

The browser and IBM Bob MCP tools use the same Python engine.
notes: The browser calls /api/analyze. engine.py loads the saved failure model, applies the selected weather scenario and scores twelve fictional assets. It returns model sensitivities, area exposure and crew proposals. server.py serves the local interface. mcp_server.py exposes the same engine to a compatible client. The real ETT temperature model is a separate evaluation track and is not an input to the failure classifier. Sources: src/engine.py, src/server.py, src/mcp_server.py.

title: The operator workspace
subtitle: Prominent inputs and inspectable outputs
body:
Edit weather conditions and crew availability, then run the analysis. Risk summaries highlight flagged equipment, expected customer exposure and jobs without a crew.

The priority watchlist opens each asset’s readings and model sensitivity. Top navigation separates maintenance planning, model evidence and the Bob connection.
notes: Screenshot: demo/screenshots/04-redesigned-overview.png, captured from the running local application. This saved screenshot shows a 55 km/h, 25 mm scenario with three crews, so its figures differ from the standard 45 km/h baseline shown later. The interface labels simulation data and shows when edited inputs have not yet been applied. Risk-weighted customer exposure is an expected value under fictional service assumptions, not a count of confirmed outages.

title: Two datasets, different claims
subtitle: Real observations and simulated failures stay separate
body:
REAL / ETTh1
Hourly transformer oil temperatures and six electrical-load variables. Used to forecast temperature 24 hours ahead. It contains no outage labels.

SYNTHETIC / 12,960 records
36 fictional assets over 360 days, with sensor readings, weather scenarios, prior incidents and stochastic next-day failures.
notes: ETTh1 comes from Haoyi Zhou and colleagues’ ETDataset, associated with Informer, AAAI 2021: https://github.com/zhouhaoyi/ETDataset. The local downloader records source hashes. The synthetic generator uses seed 42 and deliberately high failure prevalence for demonstration. It is not a physical reliability simulator: consecutive events can occur, and it does not model repairs or resets. The real-data forecast cannot establish outage accuracy, and synthetic classifier performance cannot establish real-world reliability. Sources: data/provenance.json, src/train.py, docs/model-card.md.

title: Training without future leakage
subtitle: Earlier periods train the model; later periods test it
body:
Temperature: standardize current readings, past temperatures, a trailing mean and time of day; train Ridge Regression.

Failures: compare Logistic Regression with Histogram Gradient Boosting. Select using validation average precision.

Chronological splits include boundary gaps. The alert threshold is chosen on validation data, not the test set.
notes: Temperature data uses an approximately 60/20/20 split after feature construction and a 24-hour embargo at each boundary. Ridge alpha values 1, 10, 100 and 1000 are compared by validation MAE; alpha 1 wins. The failure split is days 0–215, 217–287 and 289–359. Logistic Regression wins validation AP 0.7448 versus 0.7305 for boosted trees. A 35% probability threshold maximizes validation F1 over a fixed grid. The test uses later periods from the same fleet, not unseen assets. Source: src/train.py and models/metrics.json.

title: Real temperature forecasting
subtitle: A modest improvement over a simple baseline
body:
The model predicts oil temperature 24 hours ahead from real transformer observations.

Test mean absolute error is 1.63°C, compared with 1.71°C when assuming the current temperature persists.

This is about a 4.7% reduction in error. It measures temperature forecasting, not outage prediction.
notes: Exact test MAE is 1.6344863°C for Ridge versus 1.7143952°C for persistence. Test contains 3,446 forecast origins. RMSE is 2.1276°C versus 2.2400°C. The nominal 90% residual interval, fitted on validation, covers 93.09% of test outcomes. Time dependence and distribution shift mean this is not a general coverage guarantee. Lower MAE is better. Source: models/metrics.json, temperature section.

title: Synthetic failure prediction
subtitle: Measured accuracy at the selected 35% alert threshold
body:
Training accuracy: 74.05% on 7,776 records.
Validation accuracy: 73.51% on 2,556 records.
Test accuracy: 72.03% on 2,556 records.

Test recall is 80.72%; precision is 63.99%. These figures describe simulated events only.
notes: Accuracy was calculated from the saved Logistic Regression model and original temporal splits at threshold 0.35. The test majority-class baseline is 56.77%. Test average precision is 0.7717 versus 0.5117 for the hand-written threshold baseline. Average precision is not the same metric as accuracy. Synthetic test prevalence is 43.23%, far above ordinary utility equipment failure rates. This demo does not establish generalization to actual field events. Sources: models/failure.joblib, data/synthetic_history.csv, models/metrics.json, prior local accuracy calculation.

title: Risk becomes a work priority
subtitle: Probability and consequence answer different questions
body:
Priority weights failure probability by effective customer exposure and critical facilities. Backup supply reduces assumed exposure.

The map and watchlist help operators locate the highest-impact assets. Feature sensitivity shows how the model responds when one input is replaced by its training median.

Sensitivity supports inspection; it does not prove a physical cause.
notes: The implemented impact weight is customers × (1 − backup fraction) + 5,000 × critical sites. Priority equals probability × impact weight. The 5,000 weight is a prototype design assumption, not an industry standard. Area exposure sums risk-weighted customers across disjoint fictional customer groups. The prototype does not model power flow, cascading failures or overlapping service areas. Feature replacement is a sensitivity analysis, not causal attribution. Source: src/engine.py.

title: A storm planning example
subtitle: More crews reduce the backlog, not equipment risk
body:
At 45 km/h wind and 25 mm rain, three crews leave two jobs unassigned.

At 85 km/h and 65 mm rain, ten assets are flagged and three crews leave six jobs unassigned.

Keeping that storm unchanged and adding three crews reduces unassigned jobs to one.
notes: These results were verified in the running application. Each crew has an eight-hour shift and either electrical or line skills. Electrical inspections take four hours plus one hour travel, and line inspections take two plus one travel. The greedy planner assigns jobs by priority to a compatible crew with capacity. Each crew stages in the area of its first job. These are proposals, not actual dispatches. Road access, routing optimization and safe access checks are outside the prototype. Sources: src/engine.py, docs/verification.md.

title: IBM Bob as the operator advisor
subtitle: Tool-backed explanations from the same analysis engine
body:
assess_grid_risk returns asset probabilities, evidence, ranked priorities and crew proposals.

get_model_evaluation returns measured results and data provenance. Bob can use both to write a grounded operator brief.

The MCP handshake and both tools passed protocol tests. A signed-in Bob application demonstration remains pending.
notes: The project includes a local stdio MCP server and a configuration generator. The dashboard itself does not contain an LLM chat service and does not claim an active Bob session. The language-model role is to explain tool results, not to invent risk scores or replace the trained classifier. Example request: assess 85 km/h wind, 65 mm rain and three crews, explain the top priorities, staging and unassigned work, then state model limitations. Sources: src/mcp_server.py, src/test_mcp.py; https://bob.ibm.com/docs/ide/configuration/mcp/mcp-in-bob.

title: What works, and what comes next
subtitle: A complete local workflow with clear validation boundaries
body:
Built and tested: trained models, scenario dashboard, priority scoring, constrained crew planning and MCP tools. Six system tests passed.

Next: obtain timestamped utility failures, maintenance histories and archived weather forecasts. Validate on later periods and unseen equipment.

Field evaluation should measure false alerts, warning lead time, probability calibration and recall at a crew budget.
notes: GridWatch can be demonstrated locally now, but it is not production-ready. Weather and grid assets are simulated; the web server is local-only; no live ingestion, operational dispatch or field outage accuracy is claimed. A clean-machine installation and signed-in Bob UI demonstration remain pending. The recommended development path is data validation followed by retrospective testing and a supervised pilot, not automatic operational control. Sources: docs/verification.md, docs/model-card.md and docs/submission-status.md.
